title: Logical properties
learningObjectives: Explain logical properties and apply the concept in maintainable CSS.

understand.concept: CSS logical properties describe layout relative to writing mode and text direction. Examples include margin-inline, padding-block, inset-inline-start, and border-block-end. They allow components to adapt to left-to-right and right-to-left writing directions more naturally than physical left/right properties.
understand.whyItMatters: Logical properties support internationalisation and different writing modes. They reduce the need for separate direction-specific stylesheets and make reusable components more adaptable.
understand.analogy: Physical properties name compass directions; logical properties name positions relative to the text's flow.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy simplifies the idea; actual cascade, inheritance, and rendering follow CSS specifications.

explain.narrative: The border is placed at inline-start, which changes according to direction and writing mode.

practise.guidedTask: Set the page direction to rtl and observe how border-inline-start and padding-inline behave. Compare with border-left.
practise.independentTask: Build a small component or page section that uses the concept. Test alternate content and, where relevant, right-to-left direction or reduced-motion settings.

Keep user preferences and writing direction in mind.

questions.prompt: Which logical property adds padding on both inline sides?
questions.explanation: padding-inline maps to the start and end sides of the inline axis.

questions.prompt: What is a maintainable way to use CSS features across a project?
options: Use clear reusable rules and test computed behaviour
Copy unrelated declarations into every component
Ignore writing direction and user preferences
questions.answer: Use clear reusable rules and test computed behaviour
questions.explanation: Reusable CSS should remain understandable and work across relevant content and user settings.
